internal_alignment: Defining versus non-defining attributes: orientation, size, and color do not change a shape; side and corner counts, equal sides, and square corners do. Counting sides and corners to name shapes; square criteria (4 equal sides, 4 square corners); composing 2D shapes from exact-fitting parts (two trapezoids make a hexagon, two half-circles make a circle). Internal record only; the printable answer key carries no standards codes or references.
model_accuracy: Every shape verified mathematically before rendering: squares and diamonds have 4 equal sides and 90 degree corners; rectangles have equal opposite sides and unequal adjacent sides; rhombuses have equal sides and no 90 degree corners; pentagons and hexagons are regular with equal sides; the trapezoid is the classic isosceles form with exactly one pair of parallel sides; the two hexagon halves are congruent trapezoids whose vertex union rebuilds the hexagon. Page 4 exact fit: hexagon side 44, trapezoid sides 44/44/44/88, target circle radius 44, half-circle radius 44, so the correct pieces are the targets' own parts at full size. Page 1 answers: triangles are the big, side-pointing, tall skinny, and pointing-down triangles (not the open shape, not the 4-sided shape); squares are the square, rotated square, big square, and small square (not the rectangle, not the rhombus). Page 2: hexagon 6/6, pentagon 5/5, trapezoid 4/4, rectangle 4/4, triangle 3/3; mystery 5/5 is a pentagon; mystery 4/4 is any two of square, rectangle, trapezoid, rhombus. Page 3: squares are the square, diamond, big square, and small square; the diamond is a square because it has 4 equal sides and 4 square corners; the rectangle is not because not all sides are equal. Page 4: (A) the two trapezoids, (A) the two half-circles, (A) the bottom trapezoid. Page 5 is open-ended: check each drawing against its rule (triangle pointing down; rectangle taller than wide; square turned like a diamond; 5-sided shape).
pack: Grade 1 Math: Shapes and Their Attributes

pages_detail.activities: Worked row of three triangles that look different but share 3 sides, 3 corners, closed; circle every triangle among six shapes (including an open shape and a four-sided distractor); circle every square among six shapes (including a rectangle and a rhombus as distractors)
answers: Triangles: big, side-pointing, tall skinny, pointing-down (not the open shape, not the 4-sided shape)
Squares: square, rotated square (diamond orientation), big, small (not the rectangle, not the rhombus)
pages_detail.title: Same Shape, Different Look

pages_detail.activities: Worked flat-top hexagon example with sides numbered clockwise 1-6 from the top edge and corner dots, captioned 6 sides, 6 corners; pentagon, trapezoid, rectangle, and triangle each with name printed below and sides/corners boxes; two mystery questions answered from counts alone
answers: Mystery 4/4: any two of square, rectangle, trapezoid, rhombus
pages_detail.title: Count the Sides and Corners

pages_detail.activities: Six marked shapes in two rows of three with side ticks and square-corner marks; circle the squares; two reasoning panels with word blanks (why a diamond IS a square; why a rectangle is NOT)
answers: Circle the squares: square, diamond, big square, small square
Why is it a square? 4 equal sides, 4 square corners
Why is it NOT a square? Not all sides are equal; the corners are square
pages_detail.title: Is It a Square?

pages_detail.activities: Three tinted panels: make a hexagon from two trapezoids, make a circle from two half-circles, and circle the missing piece of a hexagon; matching pieces shown unassembled; every choice group labelled A, B, C; correct pieces at exact target scale
pages_detail.title: Put Shapes Together

pages_detail.activities: Four large drawing boxes (2x2): triangle pointing down; diamond-turned square; tall skinny rectangle; 5-sided shape
answers: Open-ended: check each drawing against its rule; count the sides together rather than correcting the drawing
pages_detail.title: Draw It My Way
